# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the seven gates,

# Host Adapter Migration Spec

This spec turns the final v2 host-adapter design into implementation goals. The
target is one host-independent Guild core that runs the full idea-to-research-to-
brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan-to-implementation lifecycle, then connects to each
host through explicit adapters. A host adapter advertises available features and
Guild uses the best primitive the host supports: native hooks first, then native
commands, then wrapper/bootstrap commands, then instruction-file guidance, then
file-bus or serial degradation. Missing host features are never silent; every
degradation is recorded in `.guild/`.

Implementation is governed by
[`17-implementation-dod-and-verification`](17-implementation-dod-and-verification.md):
each run must define done, produce evidence, pass tests, pass Claude review, and
close followups before the migration can be called verified.

The current verified state is mixed: the plugin can render package trees for
Claude Code, Codex, `.agents`, Pi, and Antigravity; tests cover several routing
and packaging paths; Guild has its own `.guild/wiki` memory layer; and tmux pane
adapters exist for multiple CLIs. But install/runtime support remains
Claude-first, non-Claude package renderers are dormant, app surfaces are mostly
type-level, settings enums are not aligned with the host registry, model effort
is parsed but not dispatched, and mixed-host tmux orchestration still has
Claude-pinned assumptions.

## Goal 0 - update final v2 docs first

**Goal.** Make `docs/v2/` the website-ready source of truth before code changes
begin, so website content can be generated from final design docs rather than
from stale implementation notes or exploratory ADRs.

**Required changes.**

- Update `07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md` to state the final adapter rule:
  hooks are preferred when a host has them; otherwise Guild degrades through
  commands, wrappers, instructions, file-bus, or serial execution.
- Update `08-dispatch-execution.md` to state that the starting host owns the
  orchestrator role; Claude is not a universal orchestrator default.
- Update `13-config-surfaces.md` to show the full host registry and model
  parameter object, including host-defined <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> axes.
- Update `15-distribution.md` to separate "package renderer exists" from
  "installable and verified on this host."
- Keep `docs/knowledge/` as provenance and ADR material. Do not move
  exploratory or audit-only text into the website-facing design set.

**Acceptance criteria.**

- The v2 docs never claim a host is installable or runtime-verified unless the
  installer and adapter path are wired and tested.
- The website can use `docs/v2/` as the final product/design corpus without
  reading `docs/knowledge/` directly for user-facing claims.
- Each v2 doc that mentions host support uses the same status vocabulary.
  During planning a row may be `target` or `detect-only`, but final migration
  support rows may only be `verified`, `unavailable`, `degraded`,
  `enqueue_only`, or `manual_instruction`, and every final status must have
  executable evidence.

# Implementation Definition of Done & Verification Plan

This document is the execution gate for the host-adapter migration. It must exist
before implementation agents are dispatched. It turns the goals in
[`16-host-adapter-migration-spec`](16-host-adapter-migration-spec.md) into
run-sized work packages, each with a definition of done, required evidence,
tests, Claude reviewer gate, documentation updates, and followup policy.

No implementation run is complete because code was merged or tests passed alone.
A run is complete only when its evidence proves the relevant spec goals, Claude
review returns no unresolved issues, tests cover the claims being made, final v2
docs are current, and all blocking and non-blocking followups from the run are
either solved or explicitly reclassified into a later run by this plan.

## Global completion gate

The full migration is verified only when all of the following are true:

1. Every goal in `16-host-adapter-migration-spec.md` has a completed run packet
   with code evidence, test evidence, documentation evidence, and review
   evidence.
2. No host support claim remains `target`, `contract-only`, `detect-only`, or
   `deferred`. The requested final state for this migration is no deferred
   functionality in the host-adapter spec. A host feature may end as
   `verified`, `unavailable`, `degraded`, `enqueue_only`, or
   `manual_instruction` only when executable evidence proves that exact state and
   the visible degradation receipt.
3. Every generated package, installer/bootstrap path, adapter path, settings
   path, memory path, dispatch path, review path, and run-record export path has
   an executable verification.
4. Claude review has been run for every implementation run and for the final
   integrated diff. All Claude findings are fixed or re-reviewed to no issue.
5. The focused automated tests and the final full verification suite pass from
   the current worktree.
6. `docs/v2/` is current and website-ready. `docs/knowledge/` remains provenance
   and ADR material only.
7. No run has unresolved followups. A followup discovered in one run either
   blocks that run or is promoted into a named later run before the first run can
   close.
8. The final support matrix is generated from tests/capability output, not hand
   written.

## Required run packet

Every implementation run must produce or update a `.guild/runs/<run-id>/`
record with these fields/artifacts before it can be verified:

- `run.yaml` with `spec_goal_ids`, `implementation_run_id`, owner, start/end
  times, active workspace/sub-project root, and host.
- `definition-of-done.md` copied from the relevant run section below, with
  task-specific details filled in.
- `evidence.md` listing files changed, exact tests run, exact reviewer command,
  docs updated, and support-matrix rows affected.
- `review/claude.md` containing the Claude reviewer prompt and output.
- `review/progress.jsonl` or equivalent run-trace entries containing
  `review_progress.v1` events for <HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED> reviewer launch,
  heartbeat, activity, error, cancellation, and final-result states when a
  reviewer was invoked.
- `followups.md` with the literal status `none` or a list of resolved followups
  and their evidence.

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

# Host Adapter Migration Spec

This spec turns the final v2 host-adapter design into implementation goals. The
target is one host-independent Guild core that runs the full idea-to-research-to-
brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan-to-implementation lifecycle, then connects to each
host through explicit adapters. A host adapter advertises available features and
Guild uses the best primitive the host supports: native hooks first, then native
commands, then wrapper/bootstrap commands, then instruction-file guidance, then
file-bus or serial degradation. Missing host features are never silent; every
degradation is recorded in `.guild/`.

Implementation is governed by
[`17-implementation-dod-and-verification`](17-implementation-dod-and-verification.md):
each run must define done, produce evidence, pass tests, pass Claude review, and
close followups before the migration can be called verified.

The current verified state is mixed: the plugin can render package trees for
Claude Code, Codex, `.agents`, Pi, and Antigravity; tests cover several routing
and packaging paths; Guild has its own `.guild/wiki` memory layer; and tmux pane
adapters exist for multiple CLIs. But install/runtime support remains
Claude-first, non-Claude package renderers are dormant, app surfaces are mostly
type-level, settings enums are not aligned with the host registry, model effort
is parsed but not dispatched, and mixed-host tmux orchestration still has
Claude-pinned assumptions.

**Goal.** Make `docs/v2/` the website-ready source of truth before code changes
begin, so website content can be generated from final design docs rather than
from stale implementation notes or exploratory ADRs.

**Required changes.**

- Update `07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md` to state the final adapter rule:
  hooks are preferred when a host has them; otherwise Guild degrades through
  commands, wrappers, instructions, file-bus, or serial execution.
- Update `08-dispatch-execution.md` to state that the starting host owns the
  orchestrator role; Claude is not a universal orchestrator default.
- Update `13-config-surfaces.md` to show the full host registry and model

- Update `15-distribution.md` to separate "package renderer exists" from
  "installable and verified on this host."
- Keep `docs/knowledge/` as provenance and ADR material. Do not move

# Host Adapter Migration Spec

This spec turns the final v2 host-adapter design into implementation goals. The
target is one host-independent Guild core that runs the full idea-to-research-to-
brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan-to-implementation lifecycle, then connects to each
host through explicit adapters. A host adapter advertises available features and
Guild uses the best primitive the host supports: native hooks first, then native
commands, then wrapper/bootstrap commands, then instruction-file guidance, then
file-bus or serial degradation. Missing host features are never silent; every
degradation is recorded in `.guild/`.

Implementation is governed by
[`17-implementation-dod-and-verification`](17-implementation-dod-and-verification.md):
each run must define done, produce evidence, pass tests, pass Claude review, and
close followups before the migration can be called verified.

Claude-first, non-Claude package renderers are dormant, app surfaces are mostly

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects
*who* reviews at the gate boundaries:

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the seven gates,
  STRONG independence when available (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies it).
- **`local`** (the shipped default) — **same-host review only; the broker is not engaged by
  mode.** The mode alone makes `review_required == false`, so the broker records

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects
*who* reviews at the gate boundaries:

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the seven gates,
  STRONG independence when available (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies it).
- **`local`** (the shipped default) — **same-host review only; the broker is not engaged by
  mode.** The mode alone makes `review_required == false`, so the broker records

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects
*who* reviews at the gate boundaries:

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the seven gates,
  STRONG independence when available (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies it).
- **`local`** (the shipped default) — **same-host review only; the broker is not engaged by
  mode.** The mode alone makes `review_required == false`, so the broker records
  `status: skipped` at each gate — though `risk ... [TRUNCATED]

# Dispatch & Execution

**Every unit of Guild work is dispatched through one neutral contract and routed
along three orthogonal axes.** A `task_run` describes *what* must happen; the
runtime then resolves **mode** (which execution backend), **tier** (which cost
class of model), and **host** (which orchestration environment) — independently,
deterministically, and on disk. Backend is resolved **once** at run-start intake
and frozen; tier is scored **per lane**; host is intersected **per dispatch**.
The work itself runs as an ephemeral one-agent-per-task §task§agent, checkpoints
after each lane so a crashed run resumes, and rolls up across waves into a
program manifest.

This doc owns the **execution mechanics**. The three *adaptability* axes — host,
substrate, and adversarial — and the degradation matrix that governs them are
defined in [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md);
08 references them and never re-spells them. The 6-phase machine that *calls*
dispatch is defined in [`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the review broker that
consumes the receipts is [`09-adversarial-review`](09-adversarial-review.md).

## The three routing axes (the model)

A single dispatch is the composition of three independent decisions. None
overrides another; each writes its outcome to disk.

| Axis | Question | Resolver | When resolved | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mode** (substrate) | tmux team · in-process agent · subagent? | D5 `agent_mode` ladder | **once** at run-start intake; frozen in the resolved-settings snapshot | v2x §D5 |
| **Tier** (cost) | cheap · mid · powerful? | complexity auto-score | **per lane** at dispatch | cost-aware §2 |
| **Host** (orchestrator) | claude-code · codex-local · codex-cloud? | deterministic capability router | **per dispatch attempt** | target-arch host_adapter |

> Mode × tier × host are **orthogonal**: adding Codex as a host is config + an
> adapter, not a redesign; switching a lane to `powerful` does not change its
> backend; pinning `agent_mode: subagent` does not change tiering. The
> *substrate* and *host* axes — and how they degrade — are the subject of
> [`07`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md).

## 1. The dispatch contract — `guild.task_run.v1`

The orchestrator writes **one `task_run` file per (re)dispatch attempt** before
the attempt runs. It is the neutral, host-agnostic description of a lane: ids,
specialist, objective, context-bundle pointer, `depends_on`, permissions,
budget, `autonomy_policy`, and the `host.capability_requirements` the router
intersects. It is **bound here by pointer, never re-spelled.**

# Config & Command Surfaces

**Guild has exactly one config file and one command grammar.** All behavior lives
in `.guild/settings.json` — a single JSON file under a closed-key reject regime,
resolved through a 7-source inheritance chain where **CLI flags always win**. All
user input is a flat-token command `/guild:<verb>` — six phase verbs plus a small
set of nouns and maintenance verbs, with **five global flags + `--dry-run`** for
the tuning surface. Skills are **model-invoked, never typed**.

This is the operator's control surface: what you type, what you set, and how the
two compose. The lifecycle the verbs drive is defined in
[`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the dispatch keys' *semantics* are in
[`08-dispatch-execution`](08-dispatch-execution.md); this doc owns the **surface**
— the file, the grammar, and the flags.

## 1. `.guild/settings.json` — the single config surface

There is **ONE config file**: `.guild/settings.json` (JSON). It replaces the v1
`.guild/config.yml` (YAML); the `config.yml` runtime reader is **removed in v2.0**
(convert a v1 file with `/guild:migrate`). JSON has no comments, so the scaffold
embeds a top-level `"_help"` block (keys prefixed `_` are reader-ignored
annotations).

**Closed-key reject regime.** Config is human-authored, so a typo must surface —
the reader is **not** lenient here (unlike the frozen `guild.*.v1` artifact
contracts). Unknown keys are **rejected at Session Intake / `--validate`**, not
silently ignored. Three rejections are absolute:

| Rule | Rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown key | any key/sub-key outside the closed set | typos must surface |
| `defaults.wiki.autopromote: true` | always rejected | agents emit knowledge **candidates only** — never auto-promote |
| `defaults.adversarial: off` | rejected for Guild self-build | self-build keeps adversarial review always-on |

**Authoring surface.** `/guild:config <init|show|validate|set|providers|update-mcp-hashes>`:
- `config init` scaffolds `settings.json` with every key = default + the `_help`
  block (idempotent — never clobbers operator config); `/guild:init` scaffolds it
  at bootstrap if absent.
- `config show` prints the resolved config; `config show --sources` annotates
  each key with the inheritance layer that won it.
- `config validate` runs the closed-key checks on the raw file; `--effective`
  validates the post-inheritance resolved config.
- `config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local` performs a scoped,
  read-modify-write **hard-set** (always-asks under auto-approve; never clobbers
  unrelated keys or `_help`; validates every dotted segment against the closed
  set before writing). The chain has two `settings.local.json` layers, so
  `--scope local` is resolved by **cwd**: it writes the resolved *project's*
  `settings.local.json`; run it from the workspace root (where the workspace and
  project layers collapse to one file, §2) to write the workspace-local layer.

  canonical host ids (`claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`,

# Distribution — Packaging & Installation

How Guild gets onto a machine. This is a design doc, not a tutorial — it binds the distribution surfaces, their guarantees, and the documentation rule that keeps every install snippet honest. Ground truth for shipped behavior: `plugin/README.md` §Getting Started, `plugin/install.sh`, and the website getting-started page.

## The four distribution surfaces

| Surface | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code marketplace** | **[v2]** | The canonical channel: `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` as a plugin marketplace; three commands install it |
| **Repo-hosted installer** | **[v2]** | `curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh \| bash` (primary) / `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh \| bash` (fallback) — host detection + marketplace install |
| **Source install** | **[v2]** | `git clone` + `claude plugin marketplace add .` + project-scoped install (development path) |
| **Per-host packaging** | `[v2]` target | Render surface 1 of the adapter contract per host. `build:hosts` renders packages/bootstrap artifacts for `claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`, `antigravity-cli`, and `agents-file`, while app/connector targets expose connector/bootstrap instructions and refuse CLI package install. |

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add <ORG_REDACTED>/guild
claude plugin marketplace update guild
claude plugin install guild@guild
```

These three lines are the contract. **Restart required:** Claude Code loads plugin commands, skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers at session startup — a freshly installed or updated plugin stays invisible until the next session. Updates flow through the same channel (`marketplace update guild` then reinstall); the GitHub repo *is* the release channel — there is no separate registry.

```bash

- `risk ≥ high`, OR

# Dispatch & Execution

**Every unit of Guild work is dispatched through one neutral contract and routed
along three orthogonal axes.** A `task_run` describes *what* must happen; the
runtime then resolves **mode** (which execution backend), **tier** (which cost
class of model), and **host** (which orchestration environment) — independently,
deterministically, and on disk. Backend is resolved **once** at run-start intake
and frozen; tier is scored **per lane**; host is intersected **per dispatch**.
The work itself runs as an ephemeral one-agent-per-task §task§agent, checkpoints
after each lane so a crashed run resumes, and rolls up across waves into a
program manifest.

This doc owns the **execution mechanics**. The three *adaptability* axes — host,
substrate, and adversarial — and the degradation matrix that governs them are
defined in [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md);
08 references them and never re-spells them. The 6-phase machine that *calls*
dispatch is defined in [`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the review broker that
consumes the receipts is [`09-adversarial-review`](09-adversarial-review.md).

## The three routing axes (the model)

A single dispatch is the composition of three independent decisions. None
overrides another; each writes its outcome to disk.

| Axis | Question | Resolver | When resolved | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mode** (substrate) | tmux team · in-process agent · subagent? | D5 `agent_mode` ladder | **once** at run-start intake; frozen in the resolved-settings snapshot | v2x §D5 |
| **Tier** (cost) | cheap · mid · powerful? | complexity auto-score | **per lane** at dispatch | cost-aware §2 |
| **Host** (orchestrator) | claude-code · codex-local · codex-cloud? | deterministic capability router | **per dispatch attempt** | target-arch host_adapter |

> Mode × tier × host are **orthogonal**: adding Codex as a host is config + an
> adapter, not a redesign; switching a lane to `powerful` does not change its
> backend; pinning `agent_mode: subagent` does not change tiering. The
> *substrate* and *host* axes — and how they degrade — are the subject of
> [`07`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md).

The starting host owns the orchestrator role by default. Claude is not a
universal orchestrator default: a Codex-started run is Codex-orchestrated, a
Pi-started run is Pi-orchestrated, and so on unless the operator or adapter
explicitly routes orchestration elsewhere. Capability routing may select other
hosts for lanes or reviewers, but it does not silently replace the starting
host's orchestration ownership.

## 1. The dispatch contract — `guild.task_run.v1`

The orchestrator writes **one `task_run` file per (re)dispatch attempt** before
the attempt runs. It is the neutral, host-agnostic description of a lane: ids,
specialist, objective, context-bundle pointer, `depends_on`, permissions,

# Host Adapter Migration Spec

This spec turns the final v2 host-adapter design into implementation goals. The
target is one host-independent Guild core that runs the full idea-to-research-to-
brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan-to-implementation lifecycle, then connects to each
host through explicit adapters. A host adapter advertises available features and
Guild uses the best primitive the host supports: native hooks first, then native
commands, then wrapper/bootstrap commands, then instruction-file guidance, then
file-bus or serial degradation. Missing host features are never silent; every
degradation is recorded in `.guild/`.

Implementation is governed by
[`17-implementation-dod-and-verification`](17-implementation-dod-and-verification.md):
each run must define done, produce evidence, pass tests, pass Claude review, and
close followups before the migration can be called verified.

The current verified state is mixed: the plugin can render package trees for
Claude Code, Codex, `.agents`, Pi, and Antigravity; tests cover several routing
and packaging paths; Guild has its own `.guild/wiki` memory layer; and tmux pane
adapters exist for multiple CLIs. But install/runtime support remains
Claude-first, non-Claude package renderers are dormant, app surfaces are mostly
type-level, settings enums are not aligned with the host registry, model effort
is parsed but not dispatched, and mixed-host tmux orchestration still has
Claude-pinned assumptions.

# Implementation Definition of Done & Verification Plan

This document is the execution gate for the host-adapter migration. It must exist
before implementation agents are dispatched. It turns the goals in
[`16-host-adapter-migration-spec`](16-host-adapter-migration-spec.md) into
run-sized work packages, each with a definition of done, required evidence,
tests, Claude reviewer gate, documentation updates, and followup policy.

No implementation run is complete because code was merged or tests passed alone.
A run is complete only when its evidence proves the relevant spec goals, Claude
review returns no unresolved issues, tests cover the claims being made, final v2
docs are current, and all blocking and non-blocking followups from the run are
either solved or explicitly reclassified into a later run by this plan.

The full migration is verified only when all of the following are true:

   with code evidence, test evidence, documentation evidence, and review
   evidence.
2. No host support claim remains `target`, `contract-only`, `detect-only`, or
   `deferred`. The requested final state for this migration is no deferred
   functionality in the host-adapter spec. A host feature may end as
   `verified`, `unavailable`, `degraded`, `enqueue_only`, or
   `manual_instruction` only when executable evidence proves that exact state and
   the visible degradation receipt.

5. The focused automated tests and the final full verification suite pass from

6. `docs/v2/` is current and website-ready. `docs/knowledge/` remains provenance

# Distribution — Packaging & Installation

How Guild gets onto a machine. This is a design doc, not a tutorial — it binds the distribution surfaces, their guarantees, and the documentation rule that keeps every install snippet honest. Ground truth for shipped behavior: `plugin/README.md` §Getting Started, `plugin/install.sh`, and the website getting-started page.

## The four distribution surfaces

| Surface | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code marketplace** | **[v2]** | The canonical channel: `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` as a plugin marketplace; three commands install it |
| **Repo-hosted installer** | **[v2]** | `curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh \| bash` (primary) / `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh \| bash` (fallback) — host detection + marketplace install |
| **Source install** | **[v2]** | `git clone` + `claude plugin marketplace add .` + project-scoped install (development path) |

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add <ORG_REDACTED>/guild
claude plugin marketplace update guild
claude plugin install guild@guild
```

These three lines are the contract. **Restart required:** Claude Code loads plugin commands, skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers at session startup — a freshly installed or updated plugin stays invisible until the next session. Updates flow through the same channel (`marketplace update guild` then reinstall); the GitHub repo *is* the release channel — there is no separate registry.

```bash

# Config & Command Surfaces

**Guild has exactly one config file and one command grammar.** All behavior lives
in `.guild/settings.json` — a single JSON file under a closed-key reject regime,
resolved through a 7-source inheritance chain where **CLI flags always win**. All
user input is a flat-token command `/guild:<verb>` — six phase verbs plus a small
set of nouns and maintenance verbs, with **five global flags + `--dry-run`** for
the tuning surface. Skills are **model-invoked, never typed**.

This is the operator's control surface: what you type, what you set, and how the
two compose. The lifecycle the verbs drive is defined in
[`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the dispatch keys' *semantics* are in
[`08-dispatch-execution`](08-dispatch-execution.md); this doc owns the **surface**
— the file, the grammar, and the flags.

## 1. `.guild/settings.json` — the single config surface

There is **ONE config file**: `.guild/settings.json` (JSON). It replaces the v1
`.guild/config.yml` (YAML); the `config.yml` runtime reader is **removed in v2.0**
(convert a v1 file with `/guild:migrate`). JSON has no comments, so the scaffold
embeds a top-level `"_help"` block (keys prefixed `_` are reader-ignored
annotations).

**Closed-key reject regime.** Config is human-authored, so a typo must surface —
the reader is **not** lenient here (unlike the frozen `guild.*.v1` artifact
contracts). Unknown keys are **rejected at Session Intake / `--validate`**, not
silently ignored. Three rejections are absolute:

| Rule | Rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown key | any key/sub-key outside the closed set | typos must surface |
| `defaults.wiki.autopromote: true` | always rejected | agents emit knowledge **candidates only** — never auto-promote |
| `defaults.adversarial: off` | rejected for Guild self-build | self-build keeps adversarial review always-on |

**Authoring surface.** `/guild:config <init|show|validate|set|providers|update-mcp-hashes>`:
- `config init` scaffolds `settings.json` with every key = default + the `_help`
  block (idempotent — never clobbers operator config); `/guild:init` scaffolds it
  at bootstrap if absent.
- `config show` prints the resolved config; `config show --sources` annotates
  each key with the inheritance layer that won it.
- `config validate` runs the closed-key checks on the raw file; `--effective`
  validates the post-inheritance resolved config.
- `config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local` performs a scoped,
  read-modify-write **hard-set** (always-asks under auto-approve; never clobbers
  unrelated keys or `_help`; validates every dotted segment against the closed
  set before writing). The chain has two `settings.local.json` layers, so
  `--scope local` is resolved by **cwd**: it writes the resolved *project's*
  `settings.local.json`; run it from the workspace root (where the workspace and
  project layers collapse to one file, §2) to write the workspace-local layer.
- `config providers detect` probes the available cross-review providers and
  canonical host ids (`claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`,
  `ant... [TRUNCATED]

# Dispatch & Execution

**Every unit of Guild work is dispatched through one neutral contract and routed
along three orthogonal axes.** A `task_run` describes *what* must happen; the
runtime then resolves **mode** (which execution backend), **tier** (which cost
class of model), and **host** (which orchestration environment) — independently,
deterministically, and on disk. Backend is resolved **once** at run-start intake
and frozen; tier is scored **per lane**; host is intersected **per dispatch**.
The work itself runs as an ephemeral one-agent-per-task §task§agent, checkpoints
after each lane so a crashed run resumes, and rolls up across waves into a
program manifest.

This doc owns the **execution mechanics**. The three *adaptability* axes — host,
substrate, and adversarial — and the degradation matrix that governs them are
defined in [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md);
08 references them and never re-spells them. The 6-phase machine that *calls*
dispatch is defined in [`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the review broker that
consumes the receipts is [`09-adversarial-review`](09-adversarial-review.md).

## The three routing axes (the model)

A single dispatch is the composition of three independent decisions. None
overrides another; each writes its outcome to disk.

| Axis | Question | Resolver | When resolved | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mode** (substrate) | tmux team · in-process agent · subagent? | D5 `agent_mode` ladder | **once** at run-start intake; frozen in the resolved-settings snapshot | v2x §D5 |
| **Tier** (cost) | cheap · mid · powerful? | complexity auto-score | **per lane** at dispatch | cost-aware §2 |
| **Host** (orchestrator) | `claude-code-cli` · `codex-cli` · `pi-cli` · `antigravity-cli` · app/connector targets | deterministic capability router | **per dispatch attempt** | target-arch host_adapter |

> Mode × tier × host are **orthogonal**: adding Codex as a host is config + an
> adapter, not a redesign; switching a lane to `powerful` does not change its
> backend; pinning `agent_mode: subagent` does not change tiering. The
> *substrate* and *host* axes — and how they degrade — are the subject of
> [`07`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md).

The starting host owns the orchestrator role by default. Claude is not a
universal orchestrator default: a Codex-started run is Codex-orchestrated, a
Pi-started run is Pi-orchestrated, and so on unless the operator or adapter
explicitly routes orchestration elsewhere. Capability routing may select other
hosts for lanes or reviewers, but it does not silently replace the starting
host's orchestration ownership.

## 1. The dispatch contract — `guild.task_run.v1`

The orchestrator writes **one `task_run` file per (re)dispatch attempt** before
the attempt runs. It is the neutral, host-agnostic description of a lane: ids,

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects
*who* reviews at the gate boundaries:

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the seven gates,
  STRONG independence when available (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies it).
- **`local`** (the shipped default) — **same-host review only; the broker is not engaged by
  mode.** The mode alone makes `review_required == false`, so the broker records

# Distribution — Packaging & Installation

How Guild gets onto a machine. This is a design doc, not a tutorial — it binds the distribution surfaces, their guarantees, and the documentation rule that keeps every install snippet honest. Ground truth for shipped behavior: `plugin/README.md` §Getting Started, `plugin/install.sh`, and the website getting-started page.

## The four distribution surfaces

| Surface | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code marketplace** | **[v2]** | The canonical channel: `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` as a plugin marketplace; three commands install it |
| **Repo-hosted installer** | **[v2]** | `curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh \| bash` (primary) / `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh \| bash` (fallback) — host detection + marketplace install |
| **Source install** | **[v2]** | `git clone` + `claude plugin marketplace add .` + project-scoped install (development path) |
| **Per-host packaging** | `[v2]` target | Render surface 1 of the adapter contract per host. `build:hosts` renders packages/bootstrap artifacts for `claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`, `antigravity-cli`, and `agents-file`, while app/connector targets expose connector/bootstrap instructions and refuse CLI package install. |

## Marketplace install `[v2]` — the three canonical commands

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add <ORG_REDACTED>/guild
claude plugin marketplace update guild
claude plugin install guild@guild
```

These three lines are the contract. **Restart required:** Claude Code loads plugin commands, skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers at session startup — a freshly installed or updated plugin stays invisible until the next session. Updates flow through the same channel (`marketplace update guild` then reinstall); the GitHub repo *is* the release channel — there is no separate registry.

The canonical artifact is `plugin/install.sh` (the plugin repo's root). It is served at the domain as the friendly primary one-liner:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh | bash
```

with raw.githubusercontent as the always-available fallback:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh | bash
```

**Domain-independent by design** (operator decision, 2026-06-11): the installer's canonical home is the GitHub plugin repo `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` — even if the guildstack.dev domain goes away, install keeps working via the raw GitHub fallback. `<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh` (the artifact served at the domain) is a **byte-identical copy** of `plugin/install.sh`, enforced by `plugin/tests/dot-guild/install-sh-equivalence.test.ts`; the website pages *display* the same one-liners, never their own variants.

# Config & Command Surfaces

**Guild has exactly one config file and one command grammar.** All behavior lives
in `.guild/settings.json` — a single JSON file under a closed-key reject regime,
resolved through a 7-source inheritance chain where **CLI flags always win**. All
user input is a flat-token command `/guild:<verb>` — six phase verbs plus a small
set of nouns and maintenance verbs, with **five global flags + `--dry-run`** for
the tuning surface. Skills are **model-invoked, never typed**.

This is the operator's control surface: what you type, what you set, and how the
two compose. The lifecycle the verbs drive is defined in
[`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the dispatch keys' *semantics* are in
[`08-dispatch-execution`](08-dispatch-execution.md); this doc owns the **surface**
— the file, the grammar, and the flags.

## 1. `.guild/settings.json` — the single config surface

There is **ONE config file**: `.guild/settings.json` (JSON). It replaces the v1
`.guild/config.yml` (YAML); the `config.yml` runtime reader is **removed in v2.0**
(convert a v1 file with `/guild:migrate`). JSON has no comments, so the scaffold
embeds a top-level `"_help"` block (keys prefixed `_` are reader-ignored
annotations).

# Host Adapter Migration Spec

This spec turns the final v2 host-adapter design into implementation goals. The
target is one host-independent Guild core that runs the full idea-to-research-to-
brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan-to-implementation lifecycle, then connects to each
host through explicit adapters. A host adapter advertises available features and
Guild uses the best primitive the host supports: native hooks first, then native
commands, then wrapper/bootstrap commands, then instruction-file guidance, then
file-bus or serial degradation. Missing host features are never silent; every
degradation is recorded in `.guild/`.

Implementation is governed by
[`17-implementation-dod-and-verification`](17-implementation-dod-and-verification.md):
each run must define done, produce evidence, pass tests, pass Claude review, and
close followups before the migration can be called verified.

The current verified state is mixed: the plugin can render package trees for
Claude Code, Codex, `.agents`, Pi, and Antigravity; tests cover several routing
and packaging paths; Guild has its own `.guild/wiki` memory layer; and tmux pane
adapters exist for multiple CLIs. But install/runtime support remains
Claude-first, non-Claude package renderers are dormant, app surfaces are mostly

is parsed but not dispatched, and mixed-host tmux orchestration still has

# Dispatch & Execution

**Every unit of Guild work is dispatched through one neutral contract and routed
along three orthogonal axes.** A `task_run` describes *what* must happen; the
runtime then resolves **mode** (which execution backend), **tier** (which cost
class of model), and **host** (which orchestration environment) — independently,
deterministically, and on disk. Backend is resolved **once** at run-start intake
and frozen; tier is scored **per lane**; host is intersected **per dispatch**.
The work itself runs as an ephemeral one-agent-per-task §task§agent, checkpoints
after each lane so a crashed run resumes, and rolls up across waves into a
program manifest.

This doc owns the **execution mechanics**. The three *adaptability* axes — host,
substrate, and adversarial — and the degradation matrix that governs them are
defined in [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md);
08 references them and never re-spells them. The 6-phase machine that *calls*
dispatch is defined in [`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the review broker that
consumes the receipts is [`09-adversarial-review`](09-adversarial-review.md).

## The three routing axes (the model)

A single dispatch is the composition of three independent decisions. None
overrides another; each writes its outcome to disk.

| Axis | Question | Resolver | When resolved | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Mode** (substrate) | tmux team · in-process agent · subagent? | D5 `agent_mode` ladder | **once** at run-start intake; frozen in the resolved-settings snapshot | v2x §D5 |
| **Tier** (cost) | cheap · mid · powerful? | complexity auto-score | **per lane** at dispatch | cost-aware §2 |
| **Host** (orchestrator) | `claude-code-cli` · `codex-cli` · `pi-cli` · `antigravity-cli` · app/connector targets | deterministic capability router | **per dispatch attempt** | target-arch host_adapter |

> Mode × tier × host are **orthogonal**: adding Codex as a host is config + an
> adapter, not a redesign; switching a lane to `powerful` does not change its
> backend; pinning `agent_mode: subagent` does not change tiering. The
> *substrate* and *host* axes — and how they degrade — are the subject of
> [`07`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md).

The starting host owns the orchestrator role by default. Claude is not a
universal orchestrator default: a Codex-started run is Codex-orchestrated, a
Pi-started run is Pi-orchestrated, and so on unless the operator or adapter
explicitly routes orchestration elsewhere. Capability routing may select other
hosts for lanes or reviewers, but it does not silently replace the starting
host's orchestration ownership.

## 1. The dispatch contract — `guild.task_run.v1`

The orchestrator writes **one `task_run` file per (re)dispatch attempt** before
the attempt runs. It is the neutral, host-agnostic description of a lane: ids,
specialist, objective, context-bundle pointer, `depends_on`, perm... [TRUNCATED]

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects
*who* reviews at the gate boundaries:

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the broker gates,
  STRONG independence when available (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies it).
- **`local`** (the shipped default) — **same-host review only; the broker is not engaged by
  mode.** The mode alone makes `review_required == false`, so the broker records
  `status: skipped` at each gate — though `risk... [TRUNCATED]

# Distribution — Packaging & Installation

How Guild gets onto a machine. This is a design doc, not a tutorial — it binds the distribution surfaces, their guarantees, and the documentation rule that keeps every install snippet honest. Ground truth for shipped behavior: `plugin/README.md` §Getting Started, `plugin/install.sh`, and the website getting-started page.

## The four distribution surfaces

| Surface | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code marketplace** | **[v2]** | The canonical channel: `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` as a plugin marketplace; three commands install it |
| **Repo-hosted installer** | **[v2]** | `curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh \| bash` (primary) / `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh \| bash` (fallback) — host detection + marketplace install |
| **Source install** | **[v2]** | `git clone` + `claude plugin marketplace add .` + project-scoped install (development path) |
| **Per-host packaging** | `[v2]` target | Render surface 1 of the adapter contract per host. `build:hosts` renders packages/bootstrap artifacts for `claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`, `antigravity-cli`, and `agents-file`, while app/connector targets expose connector/bootstrap instructions and refuse CLI package install. |

## Marketplace install `[v2]` — the three canonical commands

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add <ORG_REDACTED>/guild
claude plugin marketplace update guild
claude plugin install guild@guild
```

These three lines are the contract. **Restart required:** Claude Code loads plugin commands, skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers at session startup — a freshly installed or updated plugin stays invisible until the next session. Updates flow through the same channel (`marketplace update guild` then reinstall); the GitHub repo *is* the release channel — there is no separate registry.

## The repo-hosted installer `[v2]` — `plugin/install.sh`

The canonical artifact is `plugin/install.sh` (the plugin repo's root). It is served at the domain as the friendly primary one-liner:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh | bash
```

with raw.githubusercontent as the always-available fallback:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh | bash
```

**Domain-independent by design** (operator decision, 2026-06-11): the installer's canonical home is the GitHub plugin repo `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` — even if the guildstack.dev domain goes away, install keeps working via the raw GitHub fallback. `<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh` (the artifact served at the domain) is a **byte-identical copy** of `plugin/install.sh`, enforced by `plugin/tests/dot-guild/install-sh-equivalence.test.ts`; the website pages *display* the same one-liners, never their own variants.

One script, canonical host ids, honest postures (the same runtime-support and
adapter ship-status split as [07](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md) §Host
roster):

- **Host detection** normalizes legacy aliases to `claude-code-cli`,

- **Claude Code CLI found** -> full marketplace install: runs the three
  canonical marketplace commands, then prints the restart instruction and first

# Config & Command Surfaces

**Guild has exactly one config file and one command grammar.** All behavior lives
in `.guild/settings.json` — a single JSON file under a closed-key reject regime,
resolved through a 7-source inheritance chain where **CLI flags always win**. All
user input is a flat-token command `/guild:<verb>` — six phase verbs plus a small
set of nouns and maintenance verbs, with **five global flags + `--dry-run`** for
the tuning surface. Skills are **model-invoked, never typed**.

This is the operator's control surface: what you type, what you set, and how the
two compose. The lifecycle the verbs drive is defined in
[`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the dispatch keys' *semantics* are in
[`08-dispatch-execution`](08-dispatch-execution.md); this doc owns the **surface**
— the file, the grammar, and the flags.

## 1. `.guild/settings.json` — the single config surface

There is **ONE config file**: `.guild/settings.json` (JSON). It replaces the v1
`.guild/config.yml` (YAML); the `config.yml` runtime reader is **removed in v2.0**
(convert a v1 file with `/guild:migrate`). JSON has no comments, so the scaffold
embeds a top-level `"_help"` block (keys prefixed `_` are reader-ignored
annotations).

**Closed-key reject regime.** Config is human-authored, so a typo must surface —
the reader is **not** lenient here (unlike the frozen `guild.*.v1` artifact
contracts). Unknown keys are **rejected at Session Intake / `--validate`**, not
silently ignored. Three rejections are absolute:

| Rule | Rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown key | any key/sub-key outside the closed set | typos must surface |
| `defaults.wiki.autopromote: true` | always rejected | agents emit knowledge **candidates only** — never auto-promote |
| `defaults.adversarial: off` | rejected for Guild self-build | self-build keeps adversarial review always-on |

**Authoring surface.** `/guild:config <init|show|validate|set|providers|update-mcp-hashes>`:
- `config init` scaffolds `settings.json` with every key = default + the `_help`
  block (idempotent — never clobbers operator config); `/guild:init` scaffolds it
  at bootstrap if absent.
- `config show` prints the resolved config; `config show --sources` annotates
  each key with the inheritance layer that won it.
- `config validate` runs the closed-key checks on the raw file; `--effective`
  validates the post-inheritance resolved config.
- `config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local` performs a scoped,
  read-modify-write **hard-set** (always-asks under auto-approve; never clobbers
  unrelated keys or `_help`; validates every dotted segment against the closed
  set before writing). The chain has two `settings.local.json` layers, so
  `--scope local` is resolved by **cwd**: it writes the resolved *project's*
  `settings.local.json`; run it from the workspace root (where the workspace and
  project layers collapse to one file, §2) to write the workspace-local layer.

  canonical host ids (`claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`,
  `ant... [TRUNCATED]

# Host Adapter Migration Spec

This spec turns the final v2 host-adapter design into implementation goals. The
target is one host-independent Guild core that runs the full idea-to-research-to-
brainstorm-to-spec-to-plan-to-implementation lifecycle, then connects to each
host through explicit adapters. A host adapter advertises available features and
Guild uses the best primitive the host supports: native hooks first, then native
commands, then wrapper/bootstrap commands, then instruction-file guidance, then
file-bus or serial degradation. Missing host features are never silent; every
degradation is recorded in `.guild/`.

Implementation is governed by
[`17-implementation-dod-and-verification`](17-implementation-dod-and-verification.md):
each run must define done, produce evidence, pass tests, pass Claude review, and
close followups before the migration can be called verified.

The current verified state is mixed: the plugin can render package trees for
Claude Code, Codex, `.agents`, Pi, and Antigravity; tests cover several routing
and packaging paths; Guild has its own `.guild/wiki` memory layer; and tmux pane
adapters exist for multiple CLIs. But install/runtime support remains
Claude-first, non-Claude package renderers are dormant, app surfaces are mostly
type-level, settings enums are not aligned with the host registry, model effort
is parsed but not dispatched, and mixed-host tmux orchestration still has
Claude-pinned assumptions.

# Dispatch & Execution

**Every unit of Guild work is dispatched through one neutral contract and routed
along three orthogonal axes.** A `task_run` describes *what* must happen; the
runtime then resolves **mode** (which execution backend), **tier** (which cost
class of model), and **host** (which orchestration environment) — independently,
deterministically, and on disk. Backend is resolved **once** at run-start intake

# Config & Command Surfaces

**Guild has exactly one config file and one command grammar.** All behavior lives
in `.guild/settings.json` — a single JSON file under a closed-key reject regime,
resolved through a 7-source inheritance chain where **CLI flags always win**. All
user input is a flat-token command `/guild:<verb>` — six phase verbs plus a small
set of nouns and maintenance verbs, with **five global flags + `--dry-run`** for
the tuning surface. Skills are **model-invoked, never typed**.

This is the operator's control surface: what you type, what you set, and how the
two compose. The lifecycle the verbs drive is defined in
[`03-lifecycle`](03-lifecycle.md); the dispatch keys' *semantics* are in
[`08-dispatch-execution`](08-dispatch-execution.md); this doc owns the **surface**
— the file, the grammar, and the flags.

## 1. `.guild/settings.json` — the single config surface

There is **ONE config file**: `.guild/settings.json` (JSON). It replaces the v1
`.guild/config.yml` (YAML); the `config.yml` runtime reader is **removed in v2.0**
(convert a v1 file with `/guild:migrate`). JSON has no comments, so the scaffold
embeds a top-level `"_help"` block (keys prefixed `_` are reader-ignored
annotations).

**Closed-key reject regime.** Config is human-authored, so a typo must surface —
the reader is **not** lenient here (unlike the frozen `guild.*.v1` artifact
contracts). Unknown keys are **rejected at Session Intake / `--validate`**, not
silently ignored. Three rejections are absolute:

| Rule | Rejected | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown key | any key/sub-key outside the closed set | typos must surface |
| `defaults.wiki.autopromote: true` | always rejected | agents emit knowledge **candidates only** — never auto-promote |
| `defaults.adversarial: off` | rejected for Guild self-build | self-build keeps adversarial review always-on |

**Authoring surface.** `/guild:config <init|show|validate|set|providers|update-mcp-hashes>`:
- `config init` scaffolds `settings.json` with every key = default + the `_help`
  block (idempotent — never clobbers operator config); `/guild:init` scaffolds it
  at bootstrap if absent.
- `config show` prints the resolved config; `config show --sources` annotates
  each key with the inheritance layer that won it.
- `config validate` runs the closed-key checks on the raw file; `--effective`
  validates the post-inheritance resolved config.
- `config set <key> <value> --scope workspace|project|local` performs a scoped,
  read-modify-write **hard-set** (always-asks under auto-approve; never clobbers
  unrelated keys or `_help`; validates every dotted segment against the closed
  set before writing). The chain has two `settings.local.json` layers, so
  `--scope local` is resolved by **cwd**: it writes the resolved *project's*
  `settings.local.json`; run it from the workspace root (where the workspace and
  project layers collapse to one file, §2) to write the workspace-local layer.
- `config providers detect` probes the available cross-review providers and
  canonical host ids (`claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`,
  `ant... [TRUNCATED]

# Adversarial Review

**Every load-bearing decision is challenged before the run moves on.** Guild puts an
independent reviewer at each gate whose only job is to force missing requirements, edge
cases, weak evidence, and unsafe assumptions into the artifact *before* execution
continues. The mechanism is the **cross-host review broker**: a host-agnostic,
bidirectional, checksum-bound review layer that sits inside the adversarial-review step of
every gate.

The headline rule is independence:

- **Cross-host review is STRONG** — the artifact's creator host and its reviewer host are
  different (Claude reviews Codex, or Codex reviews Claude). This is the full-featured
  default.
- **Same-host fallback is WEAK** — when no other host is available, a fresh-context
  same-host subagent reviews. This is **always marked `independence: weak` and recorded in
  the trail**; it is never a silent substitution.

This doc owns the review **mechanism, broker, gates, loop control, and artifact bus**.
*Which* host can review which — the host × adversarial pairing and the degradation matrix —
is owned by [`07-host-adversarial-adaptability`](07-host-adversarial-adaptability.md); 09
references it for pairing and degradation signals.

## The review broker

The broker (`guild:review-broker`) is a **loop-layer policy component, NOT a phase**. It
wraps and generalizes the legacy one-way `guild:codex-review` adapter **bidirectionally** —
Claude-origin→Codex-review AND Codex-origin→Claude-review, because Claude and Codex are
co-equal hosts. All lifecycle gates invoke the broker; `guild:codex-review` is demoted to an
internal Codex adapter (runs without the broker skill fall back to the legacy
Claude-origin-only path).

> **Gate ownership (resolves DQ-3).** Only **G-lane** is command-visible — it fires per-lane during `build` (so `build`'s skill set owns the review step). **G-spec** and **G-plan** are **skill-internal**: they fire inside `guild:brainstorm` (the ideate boundary) and `guild:plan` (the plan boundary), which is why they don't appear in `build`'s skill row — they belong to `ideate`/`plan`. G-init / G-quality / G-operations likewise fire inside their phase skills. Each producer skill wires the broker at its own review boundary (→ [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md)).

The broker is **policy-gated, not always-on**. It fires only when:

- `risk ≥ high`, OR
- `review:cross` / `--review=cross` is set (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies `--review=cross`),
  OR
- project config requires it.

When the gate does not require review, `review_required == false` → the broker resolves
`status: skipped` and the gate passes without a reviewer. **Self-build runs treat Codex
review as always-on; plugin users get it as opt-in.**

### Review modes — what `--review=local|cross|off` means

`--review` (default **`local`** — [13-config-surfaces](13-config-surfaces.md) §4) selects
*who* reviews at the gate boundaries:

- **`cross`** — engages the broker above: a different-family reviewer at the broker gates,
  STRONG independence when available (`--rigor=deep` auto-implies it).
- **`local`** (the shipped default) — **same-host review only; the broker is not engaged by

# Distribution — Packaging & Installation

How Guild gets onto a machine. This is a design doc, not a tutorial — it binds the distribution surfaces, their guarantees, and the documentation rule that keeps every install snippet honest. Ground truth for shipped behavior: `plugin/README.md` §Getting Started, `plugin/install.sh`, and the website getting-started page.

## The four distribution surfaces

| Surface | Status | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code marketplace** | **[v2]** | The canonical channel: `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` as a plugin marketplace; three commands install it |
| **Repo-hosted installer** | **[v2]** | `curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh \| bash` (primary) / `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh \| bash` (fallback) — host detection + marketplace install |
| **Source install** | **[v2]** | `git clone` + `claude plugin marketplace add .` + project-scoped install (development path) |
| **Per-host packaging** | `[v2]` target | Render surface 1 of the adapter contract per host. `build:hosts` renders packages/bootstrap artifacts for `claude-code-cli`, `codex-cli`, `pi-cli`, `antigravity-cli`, and `agents-file`, while app/connector targets expose connector/bootstrap instructions and refuse CLI package install. |

## Marketplace install `[v2]` — the three canonical commands

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add <ORG_REDACTED>/guild
claude plugin marketplace update guild
claude plugin install guild@guild
```

These three lines are the contract. **Restart required:** Claude Code loads plugin commands, skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers at session startup — a freshly installed or updated plugin stays invisible until the next session. Updates flow through the same channel (`marketplace update guild` then reinstall); the GitHub repo *is* the release channel — there is no separate registry.

## The repo-hosted installer `[v2]` — `plugin/install.sh`

The canonical artifact is `plugin/install.sh` (the plugin repo's root). It is served at the domain as the friendly primary one-liner:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://guildstack.dev/install.sh | bash
```

with raw.githubusercontent as the always-available fallback:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh | bash
```

**Domain-independent by design** (operator decision, 2026-06-11): the installer's canonical home is the GitHub plugin repo `<ORG_REDACTED>/guild` — even if the guildstack.dev domain goes away, install keeps working via the raw GitHub fallback. `<HIGH_ENTROPY_REDACTED>.sh` (the artifact served at the domain) is a **byte-identical copy** of `plugin/install.sh`, enforced by `plugin/tests/dot-guild/install-sh-equivalence.test.ts`; the website pages *display* the same one-liners, never their own variants.
